{{Short description|Mathematical object in category theory}}
In the mathematical field of [[category theory]], a '''subobject classifier''' is a special object <math>\Omega</math> of a category such that, informally, the [[subobject]]s of any object <math>X</math> correspond to the morphisms from <math>X</math> to <math>\Omega</math>. This provides an analogue of the set of [[Boolean domain|Booleans]] <math>\{0, 1\}</math> in categories other than the [[category of sets]].

The main use of subobject classifiers is in [[topos theory]], where an [[elementary topos]] is defined as a category with a subobject classifier and certain additional requirements. In the [[internal language]] of an elementary topos, the subobject classifier is used to interpret truth values, hence the alternative name “object of truth values”.

== Introduction ==

Let <math>X</math> be a set. A subset <math>Y \subseteq X</math> can be equivalently described by its [[indicator function]]

<math display=block>
\begin{align}
\chi_Y : X &\to \{0, 1\}
\\ x &\mapsto \begin{cases}1 \text{ if } x \in Y \\ 0 \text{ if } x \notin Y\end{cases}
\end{align}
</math>

Informally, subsets of <math>X</math> can be identified with functions <math>X \to \{0, 1\}</math>. A subobject classifier <math>\Omega</math> of a [[Category (mathematics)|category]] <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is an object which plays a similar role as <math>\{0, 1\}</math> does in the [[category of sets]]: subobjects of an object <math>X</math> can be identified with morphisms from <math>X</math> to the subobject classifier. To recover the subset with indicator function <math>\chi</math> in a “purely categorical way”, one can take a [[pullback (category theory)|pullback]]

<math display=block>
\begin{array}{lcl}
& Y & \rightarrow & \{1\} & \\
& \downarrow && \downarrow \\
& X & \underset{\chi}\rightarrow & \{0, 1\} & \\
\end{array}
</math>

where the function from <math>\{1\}</math> to <math>\{0, 1\}</math> is the [[inclusion map]]. Indeed, the subset <math>Y := \{x \in X \mid \chi(x) = 1\}</math>, equipped with the [[inclusion map]] <math>Y \to X</math> (and the unique, constant map <math>Y \to \{1\}</math>) is such a pullback because it has the correct universal property since a map into <math>X</math> which gives the constant function 1 when composed with <math>\chi</math> is the same as a map into <math>Y</math>.

== Definition ==

Let <math>\mathcal{C}</math> be a [[finitely complete category]] (we denote the [[terminal object]] by <math>1</math>). A '''subobject classifier''' in <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is an object <math>\Omega</math> together with a [[monomorphism]] <math>\operatorname{true} : 1 \hookrightarrow \Omega</math>{{efn|Every morphism out of the terminal object is automatically a monomorphism. This condition is included as a reminder that any pullback of <math>\operatorname{true}</math> will be a monomorphism.}} such that every monomorphism is uniquely a pullback of <math>\operatorname{true}</math>.{{sfn|Mac Lane|Moerdijk|1992|p=32}} This means that for every monomorphism <math>\iota : Y \hookrightarrow X</math>, there exists a unique morphism <math>\chi_\iota : X \to \Omega</math>, called the '''characteristic function''' or '''classifying map''' of <math>\iota</math>, such that the following diagram is a [[pullback square]] (where <math>!</math> denotes the unique morphism into the terminal object <math>1</math>):

[[File:Subobject classifier diagram.svg|center|frameless|upright=0.75|alt=A commutative diagram with morphisms ! : Y → 1, true : 1 ↪ Ω, ι : Y ↪ X and χ_ι : X → Ω]]

Equivalently (assuming <math>\mathcal{C}</math> is [[Locally small category|locally small]]), a subobject classifier is an object <math>\Omega</math> which [[Representable functor|represents]] the [[Subobject|subobject functor]] <math>\operatorname{Sub} : \mathcal{C}^\operatorname{op} \to \operatorname{Set}</math>. That is, there exists a bijection, [[Natural transformation|natural]] in <math>X \in \mathcal{C}</math>, between subobjects of <math>X</math> and morphisms <math>X \to \Omega</math>. When starting from this definition, one can recover the monomorphism <math>\operatorname{true} : 1 \hookrightarrow \Omega</math> as the subobject of <math>\Omega</math> corresponding to the morphism <math>\operatorname{id} : \Omega \to \Omega</math>.{{sfn|Mac Lane|Moerdijk|1992|p=33}}

== Further examples ==

=== Sheaves of sets ===
The category of [[sheaf (mathematics)|sheaves]] of sets on a [[topological space]] ''X'' has a subobject classifier Ω which can be described as follows:  For any [[open set]] ''U'' of ''X'', Ω(''U'') is the set of all open subsets of ''U''.  The terminal object is the sheaf 1 which assigns the [[Singleton (mathematics)|singleton]] {*} to every open set ''U'' of ''X.'' The morphism η:1 → Ω is given by the family of maps η<sub>''U''</sub> : 1(''U'') → Ω(''U'') defined by η<sub>''U''</sub>(*)=''U'' for every open set ''U'' of ''X''.  Given a sheaf ''F'' on ''X'' and a sub-sheaf ''j'': ''G'' → ''F'', the classifying morphism ''χ<sub> j</sub>'' : ''F'' → Ω is given by the family of maps ''χ<sub> j,U</sub>'' : ''F''(''U'') → Ω(''U''), where ''χ<sub> j,U</sub>''(''x'') is the union of all open sets ''V'' of ''U'' such that the restriction of ''x'' to ''V'' (in the sense of sheaves) is contained in ''j<sub>V</sub>''(''G''(''V'')).

Roughly speaking an assertion inside this topos is variably true or false, and its truth value from the viewpoint of an open subset ''U'' is the open subset of ''U'' where the assertion is true.

=== Presheaves ===
Given a small category <math>C</math>, the category of [[presheaves]] <math>\mathrm{Set}^{C^{op}}</math> (i.e. the [[functor category]] consisting of all contravariant functors from  <math>C</math> to <math>\mathrm{Set}</math>) has a subobject classifer given by the functor sending any <math>c \in C</math> to the set of [[Sieve (category theory)|sieves]] on <math>c</math>. The classifying morphisms are constructed quite similarly to the ones in the sheaves-of-sets example above.

=== Elementary topoi ===
Both examples above are subsumed by the following general fact: every [[elementary topos]], defined as a category with finite [[Limit (category theory)|limits]] and [[power object]]s, necessarily has a subobject classifier.<ref>Pedicchio & Tholen (2004) p.8</ref> The two examples above are [[Topos|Grothendieck topoi]], and every Grothendieck topos is an elementary topos.

== See also ==

* [[Quasitopos]], a type of category with a ''strong subobject classifier'', which only classifies strong subobjects
